proof:
# A sharp Doignon bound for covers which capture whole fibers

Let C be a convex body in R^n x R^d, n>=1,d>=0, and suppose
S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d) is nonempty. Put

    q=dim_H S=max_(C_z nonempty) dim_aff C_z,
    P={z in Z^n: dim_aff C_z=q},
    w_z=H_q(C_z) for z in P,
    M=H_q(S)=sum_(z in P) w_z.

There are only finitely many nonempty integer fibers. Each maximal
dimensional compact convex fiber has positive finite H_q measure;
the lower-dimensional fibers have zero H_q measure. When q=0 every
nonempty fiber is a singleton and H_0 counts it. Distinct fibers are
disjoint isometric copies of their continuous sections, so the displayed
fiber-sum identity is exact and 0<M<infinity. In particular P is finite
and nonempty. For q=d this is ordinary mixed d-volume.

Let H_1,...,H_N be closed ambient
halfspaces, with no restriction on their orientations. Assume that
for each z in P, at least one H_i captures the whole z-fiber up to
intrinsic H_q measure zero:

    for every z in P, some i has H_q(C_z intersect H_i)=w_z. (1)

Then at most 2^n of these ORIGINAL halfspaces still have property (1).
Consequently,

    max_i mu(H_i) >= M/2^n,                              (2)

where mu(A)=H_q(S intersect A) is the actual intrinsic measure. No auxiliary cap,
boundary shift, or selected point outside S appears in this theorem.

This is stronger than requiring every cap to have fiber fraction zero
or one: other caps may slice a fiber, provided some member captures it
entirely. In particular it applies to a cover of S up to mu-null sets
in which no member genuinely slices any positive-measure fiber.

## 1. Positive fibers and positive uncaptured remainders are integer convex

First,

    conv(P) intersect Z^n = P.                           (3)

Indeed, represent any integer z in conv(P) as a finite convex
combination z=sum t_l z_l, with strictly positive coefficients after
discarding zero coefficients. Convexity of C gives

    sum t_l C_(z_l) subset C_z.

Each summand has affine dimension q. Fixing points in all but one
positive-weight summand shows that the Minkowski combination has
dimension at least q. Since z is integer, C_z has dimension at most q
by the definition of q. It therefore has dimension exactly q, proving
(3). For q=0 the same argument simply retains a nonempty point.
The direction spaces of different fibers need not be assumed equal:
if a combination enlarged their dimension, its inclusion in C_z
would contradict maximality of q. Compactness of C makes P finite.

For one given closed cap H, put

    Q_H={z in P: H_q(C_z minus H_z)>0}.

The stronger identity

    conv(Q_H) intersect Z^n = Q_H                        (4)

also holds. To prove it, write H={a.z+u.x>=b}. For each z_l in Q_H,
the set

    E_l={x in relint C_(z_l): a.z_l+u.x<b}

has nonempty relative q-dimensional interior. For q>0, positive
H_q measure of the strict negative portion supplies such a point
because the relative boundary of a q-dimensional convex body is
H_q-null; continuity of the strict inequality then supplies a relative
ball. For q=0 take the strictly negative singleton. This also handles
u=0, or a continuous normal constant on the fiber's affine hull:
when such a fiber belongs to Q_H, its whole affine section has
strict negative margin.

If z=sum t_l z_l is integral, every point in sum t_l E_l belongs to
C_z and has strictly negative cap margin, by affinity. The Minkowski
combination contains a relative q-dimensional ball, by fixing points
in all but one summand. Its containing integer fiber C_z has dimension
exactly q by the same dimension argument as above. Hence the ball
has positive H_q measure and the uncaptured part of C_z does too.
For q=0 its point has positive counting measure. This proves (4),
including the case that a limiting cap hyperplane contains an entire
positive-measure fiber. If Q_H is empty, use the
convention conv(empty)=empty and (4) remains valid.

The use of strict negative remainders is deliberate. A whole intrinsic
fiber on the boundary of a closed halfspace is captured completely,
as it should be; it does not enter Q_H. No positive boundary mass is
removed or assigned to the wrong side.

## 2. Doignon applied to the actual uncaptured-base sets

For each i set B_i=conv(Q_(H_i)). These are compact convex polytopes,
possibly empty, contained in conv(P). Assumption (1) says

    intersection_i Q_(H_i) = empty.

By (4), an integer point in intersection_i B_i would belong to every
Q_(H_i), which is impossible. Thus the convex sets B_i have an
integer-free intersection. Doignon's theorem supplies a subfamily
I of size at most 2^n whose intersection is still integer-free.

For any z in P, some i in I has z notin B_i, and hence z notin
Q_(H_i). That is exactly the full-capture assertion in (1) for this
subfamily. Summing its cap masses counts every positive fiber at
least once, up to its null uncaptured parts:

    M <= sum_(i in I) mu(H_i) <= |I| max_i mu(H_i).

This proves (2). All sums over fibers are finite; fibers of dimension
less than q contribute zero to M and to every cap mass. They have
not been discarded when q=0 or when they carry the relevant H_q mass.

## 3. Exact no-slicing consequence and scope

Suppose instead the original family merely covers S up to mu-null
sets, and each cap has on each positive fiber a fraction in {0,1}.
For a fixed positive fiber, finite null captured pieces cannot cover
its positive mass. At least one cap fraction must therefore be one.
This gives (1) and proves (2).

More generally, if every original cap has mass strictly less than
M/2^n, there is an actual positive-measure fiber with a positive
uncaptured remainder for EVERY member of the family. This is the
contrapositive of the theorem. If the caps cover S, their nonempty
traces on that fiber must include genuinely partial cuts; the fiber
cannot be covered solely by full-or-empty cap traces.

The theorem does not assert that a partial-fiber cover admits a
2^n-member subcover. The sets Q_H record individual uncaptured
remainders, whose mutual intersection inside a fiber may be empty.
Confusing separate nonempty remainders with one common remainder
would incorrectly remove the continuous Helly factor. No fractional
analogue of (4) is asserted.

## 4. Sharpness and boundary cases

For d>=1 let C=[0,1]^n x K with any positive-volume d-dimensional convex body
K. For each cube vertex v put a_v=(2v_1-1,...,2v_n-1), and use the
vertical cap

    H_v={ (z,x): a_v.z >= a_v.v-1/2 }.

On the binary vertex set, a_v.z=a_v.v minus the Hamming distance
from v. Thus H_v captures precisely the entire fiber over v. These
2^n caps cover S, each has mass M/2^n, and no smaller subfamily covers
all positive fibers. This proves sharpness of both conclusions. For
d=0 take S={0,1}^n and the same vertical caps; the counting-measure
argument is identical.

For n=0, there is just one possible base; assumption (1) directly
gives a cap of full mass and a one-member subcover, consistent with
2^0=1. The preceding proof already includes q=0 and therefore d=0,
including all closed-halfspace boundary points. The simultaneous
n=d=0 case is outside the task but presents no additional issue for
this lemma.

No degeneracy approximation, thickening, affine normalization, or
conversion to ambient volume is used. The full OC assertion, including
the quantitative effect of genuine slicing on many fibers, is not
proved by this note.
